projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Suzanne Schlegel was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: This is Allison Johnson. It is October 29 2006. I'm interviewing Suzanne Schlegel at her home in Fredericksburg Virginia for the Veteran's History Project for the Library of Congress. Her date of birth is December 18th 1915. And we are going to be talking about the home front and the places that she lived during the war while her husband was in the Navy. Okay, so we can start our questions now.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Is this being recorded?

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: It's being recorded. So, um, I guess the first thing that I wanted to know was when you... why did you move to Washington [D.C.]?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Well, I had to work, I got a job there. Well it was called Office Production Management the first time. Then they changed it to War Production Board when they were talking about the war, so that's where I ended up.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So, you were already married when you...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, I wasn't. I got married... I met him [she is referring to her husband Carl Schlegel who was interviewed on the same day] in Washington.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh, wow and you are both from New York?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yes, he's from Yonkers and I'm from the nice, nice part of the state. He's in the other side...

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: From the yucky part? Well that's handy that y'all both were from the same place. So what was your job, like specifically what did you do?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I worked in the ID department where I had to get ID's for men that had to go to different industries uh to investigate them to see if they would be appropriate for, I think, war production. So I had to get their clearances, get their ID's, and then clear them through the Navy or the, uh, the army department, just to the places they were going to go.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Okay, and when did you start working there?

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Like, after the war started or...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, I, the war was just in progress I guess. Yeah, about '42 I think it was.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Okay, so right at the beginning.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah. Right from the beginning, yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: And so you actually moved to Washington in...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: '41. It was quiet then yet. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: A little bit was starting to happen then I'm sure. All ready.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, but we didn't hear about it. You know we asked the men about that and they wouldn't say anything. They said, "Well, maybe it'll happen, maybe it won't." You know. They weren't sure, they wouldn't say anything. Of course when the called the War Department or the Navy Department, but they wouldn't say anything to me.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: The guys would flirt. [Both laugh]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah, that's all they are usually good for. So how did you meet Carl?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh, that was interesting. We went to an all-state dance in one of the hotels in Washington, where each state had a certain day that people from that state would come and meet and I have, I had seven room mates.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: And we got along pretty well, and we went out to the dance together and he was there and the other guys were there and we were just dancing around and having a good time.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: You had, so, what kind of place did you live in to have seven room mates?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: It was a, lets see, first was a boarding house then, uh, the other, the rest of the... then I got in touch with all the girls from my home town. Some of them lived there already and some had some friends coming and one... a couple of them's sisters coming. So they decided, well, maybe we ought to get together and live in an apartment. So we had, uh, two bedrooms with double beds. Then we had to change...switch around, who's going to sleep on the couch, who's going to sleep on that bed, who's going to sleep on that bed...

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah, because that's a lot of people in one...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, we got along pretty... the girls from my hometown got along fine. Then they asked a girl from New York City to come and she was always sort of a spoiled brat. She wouldn't take turns to do the house cleaning, she wouldn't take turns to do the cooking, uh she was just, she thought she was a queen. [Suzanne laughs]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: There's always one of those.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I know it.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: I lived with four and we had one of those too so...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, they do yeah. But we got along pretty well, I mean, considering that there was seven of us. Well, there were two groups of sisters so one could correct the other and I guess the older one could correct the younger one.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah. So when you met Carl was he already in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: He was in the Navy, yeah he was going to the school in Navy... uh Radio Material School I think it was. In the Navy... learning about... whatever. [Suzanne laughs]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: And so when you two married what kind of place did you...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Then, uh, he got transferred to Gulf Port, Mississippi. To a school he was teaching... then he was teaching there at the school in Gulf Port, Mississippi. And then, um, let's see, we had a baby there and before we left the baby died at sixteen months and he was being transferred to a ship, so I went back to my fam... my parents, so...

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: In a ship where?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: In a ship... in the Pacific but I can't... I don't know the name on the ship.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's fine.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So, um, I guess one of the things I was kind of curious about, when I found out that I was going to be interviewing someone that was here when it happened was, you know, like nowadays everyone is like... everyone remembers where they were on September 11th and...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I re... yeah, I remember. I was, uh.... Some of us went to Washington, uh right, right to, you know where the mall is, to walk around and everything. And as we were coming back we heard commotions and got back to the apartment and said well, Pearl Harbor got bombed. So that was on a Sunday afternoon, it was a beautiful day. And we could... you know, everybody got excited then. You know, what are going to do, well you just keep on going what you're doing.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: I guess so.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: And then what about, do you remember where you where when you found out that Carl had to...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I didn't know him then... yeah, uh no, wait a minute...

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: When he found out...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, I met him after that. I met him after that, yeah. I met him at the... when he was going to school, so he was... he was off the ship that he was on. Oh, I have to reverse now... he was off the ship and he was going to the school in Radio Material School and that's where I met him and then he, then he went to teach in Gulfport, Mississippi. And then he had to go on another ship, and I can't remember the name of the ship. We were married then. Okay.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's fine. And then, when you lived in Washington, before you got married, do you remember, I mean like after Pearl Harbor did you have to do the kind of, like the air drills and that kind of stuff, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, not too much, no...

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: None of that?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, no. I remember one time, though, I was late for work. I missed the bus. And I had to walk all the way from Columbia Road all the way to the mall. I was hurrying, hurrying, hurrying, and streets were empty. I couldn't figure what's... why the streets were empty. But I had to go to my building. So I crossed the street, pretty soon a policeman comes, he says. "You are not supposed to be here. [Laughter] What are you doing here?" I said, "I'm going to work." Tears are coming down my eyes. I said, "I'm going to work, because I'm late." He said, "You're not supposed to be here." And he didn't tell me why. But President Roosevelt was supposed to be coming down the road. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh my gosh, and you were just out running around?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I wasn't running around, I was running to work because I was late.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh my goodness.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: So I didn't find that out for a long time, why he pulled me out, but... I was so upset.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah. Do you remember, speaking of FDR, do you remember the fireside chat type thing that he did during the war or listening to him on the radio?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I didn't listen to much of that, yeah once in a while we listened to it, but not too much.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Not really? Because in school, you know they teach you....

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: You know, young kids don't, not interested in that.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah. Let's see...Okay, and when Carl got shipped away and you moved back to New York, how long a period was that?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: It was, well, I can't remember. I should have written it down, but I don't remember. But about a year, then he got sick on his ship and he got, eventually he got a medical discharge. He was in the Navy for nine and a half years and he got medical discharge, so but we lived in... yeah I did meet him when his ship came in in Seattle, Washington. Was it Seattle? Yeah, way up. [Laughter] Yeah we met and then lived there for a while, while he was in the hospital. Then he was transferred to a hospital in California, Corona, California. And then we came back to New York state and lived with my parents for a while. Then rented a house. Then he finally got a... well he worked in a radio station for a while. Then he got a job at GE in Schenectady, so we moved to Schenectady... Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: You've moved all over the place!

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I don't think so. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: I don't know, that's a whole lot more places than I've ever lived.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I don't think so... I, what I wanted to do is be able to see the whole country here. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Didn't get that far?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Didn't do it.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So what was it like, to have to just be able to move, you know, on a moments notice?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Well, you forget what you have, you leave you things, you don't know where to put the stuff. It was interesting though, in Gulfport, Mississippi you know where there was the latest flooding. I lived not too far from the ocean, from the Gulf. So I think all those buildings are probably messed up now this last time.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: For Katrina.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah. But it was interesting and you meet different people. And you enjoy... interesting to talk to them and their feelings about the north. [Laughter] And all that, you know how it is. And, but I enjoyed it as far as, you know, we could. We went to a picnic one time, I have to tell you this one. We went to a picnic sometime and everybody had to bring something so I brought a nice roast pork, used my stamps for the meat, fixed it up nice. Then the guys wanted to play some games so we put the food on the side and went to watch them, came back my roast pork was done... gone. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh no!

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: The dogs came along and ate it. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh my gosh! And all that hard work...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh yeah! And I still can taste how good it was. Oh well

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Um, that's also, the rationing thing too, I'm interested in that. Because I don't think that I would know what to do with myself if I had to deal with, like rationed items and stuff like that. Was everything rationed or...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Most of the stuff, I think I have the ration coupons, oh I have to... I'll show them to you. They have a stamp, you know and you were allowed a certain amount of food, like meats, sugar, and I don't know what other stuff, but uh sugar and meats you have to... you couldn't get as much as you wanted to. So, you know losing that pork was....

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah, it was a big deal. Do you remember, um, like rationing or saving anything else to go towards the war effort, like, besides food? Materials or anything?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Um, no, nothing, no. We weren't... clothes we could buy yet and everything like that. I should tell you that we, when we took the bus or trolley to work we could get a pass for a dollar and a quarter a week. And you could go anywhere on that for the whole week.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh wow.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: A dollar and a quarter, how much does it cost you now? [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That... not that much. Um, not a dollar and a quarter...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: That costs you one day.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah, not even.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh yeah, so there was one thing I should have... well I couldn't save the tickets because you had to turn them in after each pass.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah, definitely not the same now.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: But, well we enjoyed it, we went to different concerts and programs all around. We weren't limited to anything like that. Just the food which was important because they figured the guys needed the food in the service. So it was okay, we didn't miss it. No.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: I think that it would be okay now it's just hard to imagine having to think about that everything that you...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Well, you had to plan, but heck you have to plan now too, don't you?

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah. Okay, so, when you moved back to New York, did you have friends whose husbands were also away, that were there?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Not New York, not in New York. Because the boyfriend that I had there he was gone, he wasn't gone but I was... we didn't correspond after a while. He went his way I went my way and all that. Most of the young people, like the boys or whatever, they were gone, they were in the service already or drafted or enlisted. My girlfriends well they were different ways and places so yeah they were there, but just you didn't get together too much I guess.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Not any kind of like, community activities or anything like that? For support or anything?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh, no, no, they didn't think about those things then. You had your parents, you stayed with your parents, your...I have four sisters, three brothers. So it was enough in our family.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Did you have brothers that had to go to war?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, no, they weren't, they weren't. They were... one of my brothers was in the national guard and the other boys, they were working. My father had a bakery at the time so they worked in the bakery and, I don't know they didn't have to get drafted or anything. No. My brother, my younger brother was in... well he's older now, but he was in National Guard for quite a while and he didn't get called in either.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Well that's good. Lucky.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Of all those kids theres only three of us left.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: My goodness.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So when you lived at home, was it, was everybody at home...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Your brothers and sisters were there too?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, yeah they were. Yeah some were married all ready and some weren't yet. Spread out, you know.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So your job that you did, you said you looked up information, background searches and that kind of stuff, when you were in Washington. When you moved to Mississippi did you keep working or...?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, I didn't because then I had the baby and he said, 'Well, I get married, my wife doesn't work.' And he never let me go to work...

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: He put his foot down. No?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Never. We managed. We managed on what... the small salary he got a month, how much did a sailor get a month? When I first met him, I think he was a private, no... he didn't have any rating, he made a hundred dollars a month. Something like that, yeah they didn't make much, you know.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I didn't get much. When I started working I... when I came out of business school, I got a job for... in a lawyer's office. You know how much I got paid?

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: How much?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Three dollars a week.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh my goodness.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Because he was just starting out, he didn't have much business. I was starting out. Ended up then I took some civil service tests, a friend had encouraged me to do that. I passed those so I got appointed to go to Washington, to work. So I was making seven dollars a week by that time. When I got to Washington I think I was making a hundred dollars a month.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's considerably more than three dollars a week.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yes. And you have to pay for your room and board and everything else, your clothing, your transportation. But we made out okay, because we were, you know, we had to be careful. We came from families that were in the Depression, well I was in the Depression too. So we knew that we had to save, we had to be economical. And use our food and money wisely. That helped out. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: When you lived in New York what did you do that got you transferred to...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I worked for the lawyer.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: I mean, how did that get you down to Washington.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: By train, I went by train.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: I mean you said you got sent...the appointment.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh yeah, they called me and I had interviews and then I was investigated by the FBI. They went around investigating everybody. Not everybody, to the neighborhood. And get... "Was she a good girl? Was she honest?" You know, everybody had high...good words for me and the guys say "Gee I should meet the girl, she must be wonderful." I thought oh no! I wasn't. They made me sound good. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Certainly, I think for an FBI investigation you were probably pretty clean.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yes I was. Well, they do... they do those. If you ever try to get a government job, they'll investigate you. Our son works for NSA and they investigated him too. There's this guy next door he's at Quantico right now and he's applying for a job somewhere and he was being investigated, but he just moved here and I didn't know a thing about him so I couldn't say anything. But he seemed like a nice fellow so... that's all I could tell them. I didn't know too much about him.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's very cool. I didn't know that they.... I didn't know how the investigation thing worked. They just interview your friends and your family and everything?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: They go, they don't tell you what they want. They just go and ask questions, "Do you know this person? Know anything bad... wrong about them? Are they...do they drink? Do they carouse around? Do they... you know, what's their reputation?" And all that and from that they gather, "It's okay, we can pass them."

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's cool. So how long did you work in Washington?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Well, we got married in forty...1943 then he got transferred to Gulfport Mississippi about a year later and that's where he went to school, to teach there for a couple of years I think it was. The baby was born in... he died in '46 so '45 I guess, yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So what did he teach, Carl?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Radio school, radio school stuff. Radio and, lets see, sonar systems I think but I am not sure. Yeah, connected with the ships because he was a radio man.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's neat. Let's see what else I have. [indistinct conversation in background] When you lived in D.C., I guess kind of before you were married, did you, I mean do you remember going to rallies or lectures or anything like that about...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh no, not too much. I didn't hear too much about that. No, not on the streets or anywhere.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I mean, its just talk because... because they were fighting in Europe and we didn't hear too much. We always read the papers, you know, what's going on. But the one in the Pacific when Japan bombed us it was a complete surprise. I mean, there was... he'll probably tell you, he was complete surprise as far as we were concerned because we thought everything was going on in Europe. So, it was a surprise.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So, you remember where you were with Pearl Harbor and everything, but do you remember where you were when D-Day happened and all that stuff?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yes, we were in Mississippi.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: You were in Mississippi? And how did you hear about it?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I think I heard it on the radio and I couldn't believe it and when he [Carl] came home I said "Is that true?" and he said "Yes!" So then people were celebrating. I mean, they were happy about that, but not on streets or anything as far as... no, because Gulfport wasn't such a big place then. But, that's right, that was quite exciting.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: And you all were still in Mississippi when that happened?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So he never got shipped out before that?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Well after he got out... well, no. No after that he went shipped out again to... I think its... I don't remember the ship, name of the ship.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's fine.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I don't remember really. One of those things.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So did you, while he was away did you keep, like lots of correspondence or...?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh yes, yes. Letters. That's the only way you could do it at the time. No telephones or no emails or anything like that, no. So we wrote to each other. And he was on a ship all the time so, off to sea, no... RRS, Radio... Rest and something else RR, rest and recuperation or whatever else like that.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So with him living on a ship how often could you all write to each other, like how often did you...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh anytime.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: You could?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, we wrote all the time.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: It works the same kind of mail way?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I don't know if they censored it. I don't think they censored it. No, because that was over. The war was over then and they didn't censor. But they did censor letters when the war was on if you wrote to someone they would censor them. They would look them over and cut...like if you said anything about the war or anything they would blank it out. But otherwise no.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So, did you have friends or anybody that put the little stars in their windows for family members away?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: There were a few. They were for some people in the city.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: But not you. You kind of lucked out that way, no brothers, no husband overseas, that's...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Well he [Carl] was. He had some bad experiences, he'll tell you about those. Yeah, when he was on the ship. He was a radio bomber, a radio bomber on the...aircraft carrier, yeah so, he'll tell you about that.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah. That's really interesting.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: But see, I didn't know him then. So it didn't bother me. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So he was... okay, so he was out in the war before you met and then he was there after the war was over.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, that's where he went to school. In Washington, Bethesda.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah, lets see, what else do I have. Did you... war bonds and that kind of stuff.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, we bought those, yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: I don't really know, how they work.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: You bought, well you could get them for a certain amount. For fifty.... Be worth fifty dollars, I think a hundred dollars, whatever and you paid a certain amount for each week, if you could afford it, or else you put the full amount for the bond which was... it was a fifty dollar bond but you didn't give the full amount for it, I think. Just, I forget what it was that you paid towards it. And then it took... it carried some interest on it after a certain amount of time and you could cash them or leave them in and it would draw some interest until, oh I don't know for how long after that, but it could get some... oh its like a what's a maybe... putting money in the bank and you get interest from the money there.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So what is the purpose of them, just...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Bonds? You use the bonds to buy for the Army, to buy supplies I think it was. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: They needed money. And the United States wasn't as rich as it is now that they can give money away.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah. So its just, like...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: It was a savings and it was also a help.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Okay, that makes a little more sense than it did.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: And then, you lived in the city so I guess victory gardens and that kind of stuff... did you?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yes, yes they had those.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: In the city even?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: In the city. In my hometown they had those, after... I forget when it was, I don't know, but we did have those. And it was little plots or whatever or the city would give people a certain amount of land and everyone would work on it and it was good.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's cool. Did you participate in that or just knew people?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I helped my neighbors. Potatoes and beans and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah. That's really cool.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, it was nice. It was nice. It was fun. I enjoyed it, that's why I like to garden. I like gardening. But our garden is gone. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah, my grandma always talks about how mad her family was when it became that you couldn't donate food that wasn't canned by some big company or something like that.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Well, that I don't know.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Well, she was just saying, you know, that they used to always can food and then donate it to needy people and she always complains about how, now, if it didn't come from a store and its not in the can with nice wrapping and everything, you can't donate it at all.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, because they are afraid of somebody getting sick or something like that.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That kind of cuts down on the amount you can personally do.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, for yourself you can do just so much and then how much can you eat? You can give it to your neighbors and all that... we got a nice can of tomatoes, I won't say who. And he says to my husband, "Let your wife try them, see if they're okay." [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh my goodness.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: They were old, you know. They were old tomatoes that they canned long ago and they were canning some new ones so they were trying to get rid of the old ones.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: And they were going to use you as their guinea pig?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, so you know where it went? The garden.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Good. You don't want to be anybody's guinea pig.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No. Not that way. Not that way that's for sure.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So when you and Carl were married was it like a fast thing because it was during the war or was it just like normal, long?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, it was sort of normal. We got married in November, decided to get... we'd known each other for a year. And, no, I came home and my mother took me and we went up and got my gown. Where is my... I have a picture of my gown. I couldn't get married in a church because I was Catholic and he was Protestant. So the priest wouldn't marry us in the church, in my hometown. So we got married in his hometown in Yonkers. My whole family came to the wedding. And it was... let me see if I can get the picture. [She tries to get up but is attached to the recorder]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: You're hooked up.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: It's okay. You can show me later.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I'll show you later, the wedding picture. No, I had a gown and we had a wedding reception and dancing and singing and everything. It was nice.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's nice.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: My whole family came and my father had a bakery and so he brought us a big... at that time they used to make fruit cakes for weddings cakes, so he brought us a big... We should have taken a picture of it but we never did. So all the way from Amsterdam to Yonkers he had to carry it in the car. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's a long way to come with a cake.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: It was. And it was the foggiest day they ever went through. They had to almost get out of the car to lead the driver.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: To be able to see everything?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: To see. It was okay. My whole family came.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Well that's very cool. How far away is Amsterdam from Yonkers?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh, at that time maybe, how many hours? Maybe five hours or something. It was a drive.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So, Washington then, did you live like actually in Washington?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah. Right near the, you know where the zoo is in Washington? Okay, we could walk to the zoo from where the girls and I lived.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: So was that weird, coming from Amsterdam, kind of smaller to come to...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: It was sort of. You had to get used to the people. To the...I always got lost in Washington because you know how its built around in a circle?

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Hold on a second... [flip tape]

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Are you recording?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Where we were... Schenectady no Syracuse, we moved from Syracuse. I forgot about living in Syracuse for a while. People were very, southern people were very cruel towards us. They wouldn't talk, no, they just ignored you.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Wow. New Yorkers and Southerners, I think don't have that good of a history.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, that's right. They are still carrying a chip on their shoulders., they should knock it off a little. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: I don't know I just, I guess for me I'm just, like, I feel like people around here act like, because you talk a certain way you must think a certain way. Or be a little bit dumber than regular people.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. That's true. I don't know what they thought about us, but I mean, it was hard to make... they say oh southern hospitality is great, you know. We came here and didn't see it, you know. Really, really something. They just ignored you. I even tried to get a job, not a job, volunteer work at the hospital and... because I used to volunteer in New York state at blood mobile and all that and children's... working with children and all that and I thought oh, they say they need volunteers, I'll... So first thing they asked me, "Are you from Virginia?" I said, "No, but I did the blood mobile work and I worked for the Red Cross, I volunteered for the Red Cross." "Well, we don't have any openings right now." Well, thanks.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Oh my goodness.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Did you do any volunteer work during the war and that kind of stuff?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No, because I was working then. So, no. But after we got married I worked... did a lot of volunteering in New York state, VA hospitals, Red Cross, Well Children Center, helped with that. And I enjoyed it, and I thought I'll come here. Since he doesn't want me to work, I'll do that. But, they didn't want me so they didn't want me.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Yeah, their loss right?

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: It is their loss. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Okay, now I think we can stop interviewing now and we can just do the release form. And thank you very much for doing my interview.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Okay. [Interruption in taping] A trolley car only costing a dollar and a quarter a week for a whole week, you know. And somebody... if somebody didn't have enough money to buy a trolley car pass at work, you know, and they wanted to go somewhere then they burrowed your pass and they could go and use it. And it worked out okay, but now I don't know.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Its not the same now.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Not the same at all.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I still, I forgot what they say it costs you now a days just to go... take the metro from Springfield to Washington. A dollar and a quarter or, I don't know how much it costs?

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: I don't know, but its definitely more of an event than it would have been.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Yeah, you're right.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: Okay, and here is the release form. And for this I have one for you to keep and one for me to keep. And its just going to be stored with the tape and the transcripts that I have to type up. And its just going to be saying that they can store this in the library of congress and that the people that work there and the people that come to look at this kind of stuff can hear your voice on the recording.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Oh they wouldn't want to hear it but that's okay. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: They will. And...

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: I don't like it myself.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: You just need to sign your name right there and then print your name and then that's all.

sp.speaker: Suzanne Schlegel
sp.p: Okay. My address or... my writing is bad too.

sp.speaker: Allison Johnson
sp.p: That's okay. Yeah you can just fill that in.
